Idiom (Izon): Abedí mọ bínị aru erí sèigha
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed negative declarative clause; animal-subject + comitative particle mọ + locative noun phrase + negative verb phrase.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: An outsider or poorly positioned person cannot defeat someone on their own ground.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: A person without local advantage should not expect to overpower the rightful or better-prepared owner.
Usage Contexts: politics; land and resource disputes; family warning; community debate; rhetorical criticism
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Niger Delta riverine imagery; based on the widely cited Ijaw saying that an iguana cannot win an aquatic battle with the crocodile.
First Example Sentence: Abei, wó bínị aru sèi bó dẹsẹ, Abedí mọ bínị aru erí sèigha.
Second Example Sentence: Ama tịbị kẹnị, arị bé ịkịyọ: Abedí mọ bínị aru erí sèigha.
Third Example Sentence: Toru kẹ nímị wò sẹ, Abedí mọ bínị aru erí sèigha, mọmọ fịẹgha.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed negative declarative clause; noun phrase + object noun + negative affective verb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A hardened or experienced person is not easily harmed by ordinary trouble.
Usage Contexts: daily speech; encouragement; conflict; hardship; elders’ advice
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Draws on swamp and alligator/crocodile imagery common in riverine Ijaw communities; parallels the cited proverb about muddy water not hurting the alligator’s eyes.
First Example Sentence: Ọrọ pọụ sè, bínị bara tọrụ kemegha; wó fịẹ arị.
Second Example Sentence: Ebiye kẹ ọgbọụ kẹnị wó, bínị bara tọrụ kemegha.
Third Example Sentence: Wárị kẹ tịbị yẹnị, bínị bara tọrụ kemegha, ama gbanị.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Balanced conditional-like clause; object-fronted noun phrase + verb + resumptive subject + repeated verb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Someone who provokes trouble will also suffer from the consequences.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Do not start a problem that will return to hurt you.
Usage Contexts: family correction; politics; gossip; workplace conflict; moral instruction
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Comparable to the Ijaw literary proverb 'he who shakes a coconut shakes himself'; it reflects communal caution against reckless provocation.
First Example Sentence: Wó tọrụ tịẹ kẹ fịyá kụrọ dẹsẹ, erí kụrọ.
Second Example Sentence: Ama kiri kẹ kịmị dọụ, fịyá kụrọ dẹsẹ, erí kụrọ.
Third Example Sentence: Nị tọbọụ mọ sẹgha; fịyá kụrọ dẹsẹ, erí kụrọ.

Idiom (Izon): Arụ fun dẹsẹ, inyó bẹlẹ bọgha
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Temporal subordinate clause plus negative existential main clause; canoe subject + capsize verb + cargo NP + negative completeness predicate.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: When a shared system collapses, losses affect everyone and nothing remains whole.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: A collective failure damages all parts of the group.
Usage Contexts: leadership; family crisis; workplace project failure; communal warning; literature
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: River and canoe imagery from Ijaw waterways; based on the cited proverb that when the canoe capsizes the cargo cannot be complete.
First Example Sentence: Arụ fun dẹsẹ, inyó bẹlẹ bọgha; ama kẹ ala fịẹ.
Second Example Sentence: Wó pẹrẹ ẹrẹ sẹ, arụ fun dẹsẹ, inyó bẹlẹ bọgha.
Third Example Sentence: Ọgbọụ kẹ tịbị fa dẹsẹ, arụ fun dẹsẹ, inyó bẹlẹ bọgha.

Idiom (Izon): Adaka mọ ama pọụ kẹ dọụgha
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative declarative clause; animal-subject + locative phrase + negative concealment verb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A powerful or obvious person cannot hide their influence, wrongdoing, or presence.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Something very obvious cannot be concealed.
Usage Contexts: sarcasm; public reputation; leadership; gossip; moral criticism
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Adapted to Izon animal imagery from the cited saying 'no elephant hides in open grassland'; Adaka is attested as 'lion' in Izon dictionary material.
First Example Sentence: Adaka mọ ama pọụ kẹ dọụgha; wó ẹrịmẹ kịmị mọ di.
Second Example Sentence: Kẹnị pẹrẹ kẹ ọgbọụ wari mu, adaka mọ ama pọụ kẹ dọụgha.
Third Example Sentence: Eri sẹgha tịn dẹsẹ, adaka mọ ama pọụ kẹ dọụgha.

Idiom (Izon): Opu kịmị dọụ dẹsẹ, ama pọụ tọbọ
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Temporal subordinate clause plus result clause; singular agent noun phrase + verb + collective subject response.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: One person’s action can affect or awaken the whole community.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: An individual act can have public consequences.
Usage Contexts: community meetings; politics; family reputation; praise; warning
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Reflects the cited cock-crow proverb: one cock belongs to one person, but its crow wakes the neighborhood.
Phonetic Transcription (IPA, Izon): [òpù kìmí dɔ̀ʊ̀ dɛ̀sɛ́ àmà pɔ̀ʊ́ tɔ̀bɔ̀]
First Example Sentence: Opu kịmị dọụ dẹsẹ, ama pọụ tọbọ; wó tịbị sẹgha.
Second Example Sentence: Ịzọn ama kẹ kẹnị tọbọụ dọụ, opu kịmị dọụ dẹsẹ, ama pọụ tọbọ.
Third Example Sentence: Bara kẹ ẹrị pẹrẹ gba, opu kịmị dọụ dẹsẹ, ama pọụ tọbọ.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed negative clause; animal subject + numeral/quantifier phrase + locative verb + negative marker.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A wise or adaptable person does not rely on only one support, patron, or option.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Keep more than one option available.
Usage Contexts: business; migration; school advice; survival strategy; family talk
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Based on the cited proverb that the monkey does not cling to a single tree; it reflects forest-river survival knowledge.
First Example Sentence: Ọrọ bara fịẹ, ogboin kẹnị tịẹ kẹgha.
Second Example Sentence: Bara tịbị kẹ wó sẹ, ogboin kẹnị tịẹ kẹgha; sẹị sụọ.
Third Example Sentence: Wó tịbị mọ kẹnị dọụ gha, ogboin kẹnị tịẹ kẹgha.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative declarative clause; pressed/urgent person subject + location-choice verb + negative suffix.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A person in urgent distress cannot afford to be overly selective.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: In an emergency, accept the available help or option.
Usage Contexts: daily speech; market talk; family advice; travel; humorous complaint
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: From riverine settlement experience; parallels the cited Ijaw saying that a pressed soul chooses no waterside.
First Example Sentence: Bịbị kịmị bínị sẹlẹgha; wó bé arụ kẹ mu.
Second Example Sentence: Fịya kẹ wó kịmị dẹsẹ, bịbị kịmị bínị sẹlẹgha.
Third Example Sentence: Wárị sụọọ gha dẹsẹ, bịbị kịmị bínị sẹlẹgha, bọ.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative impersonal clause; body-part metaphor noun + locative postposition + negative measurement verb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: No one can fully know another person’s hidden intention.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: A person’s inner thoughts are difficult to measure.
Usage Contexts: trust; marriage; politics; negotiation; literature; suspicion
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Draws on the cited Ijaw proverb that no pole can compute the heart’s depth; it encodes caution about unseen motives.
First Example Sentence: Toru kẹ bẹlẹ dọụgha; wó kịmị kpọụ fịẹ ma.
Second Example Sentence: Eri ẹrẹ sẹ dẹsẹ, toru kẹ bẹlẹ dọụgha, arị yẹnị.
Third Example Sentence: Ala kẹ wó tịbị tịẹ, toru kẹ bẹlẹ dọụgha.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative existential clause; small-animal subject + trap/location phrase + negative escape predicate.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: A weak or careless person cannot easily escape a trap prepared by stronger opponents.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Someone in a well-prepared trap has little chance of escape.
Usage Contexts: politics; gossip; legal conflict; warning; narrative suspense
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Based on the cited Ijaw proverb that no fly escapes a waiting spider’s web; it reflects caution against entering visible danger.
First Example Sentence: Fịní mọ dọụ bọgha; wó tịbị sẹị ma, abei.
Second Example Sentence: Eri ama kẹ ịkịyọ gbara dẹsẹ, fịní mọ dọụ bọgha.
Third Example Sentence: Wó ẹrịmẹ wárị mu dẹsẹ, fịní mọ dọụ bọgha.
